## This game

Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

# Game 10: White vs 20k — W+10

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 63–64. There were 64 moves: 61 stone moves and three passes (61, 63, 64).
Final captures: Black 0, White 4. No ko, invalid move, resignation or dead-stone removal occurred.

This is the first win in the series, following five losses at 20k. It establishes one successful game at 20k, not consistent strength or an optimal opening. Retain 20k until wins and living groups are repeatable, including as Black.

## Records and verified score
- game-010.sgf contains all 64 moves.
- game-010-log.json contains opponent selection, all 32 play responses, every returned board, current-board group/liberty inventories, complete moves and independent area count.
- Official result: White wins by 10 points.
- Independent final-board count: Black 26 stones + 13 territory = 39; White 31 stones + 11 territory = 42. White plus komi = 49. All 81 points are assigned; no neutral points.
- White's lower group: 14 stones plus E1/D2/D3 = 17 area.
- White's upper group: 17 stones plus A9/C8/D9/E9/F9/G9/H9/J9 = 25 area.
- Upper area by rows: all nine points in row 9, all nine in row 8, B7/C7/D7/E7/G7 (five), and C6/D6 (two): 25.
- Black territory: A5 and H1/J1/H2/J2/H3/J3/H4/J4/G5/H5/J5/J6.
- Black captured no White stones. The four captured Black stones were E1 at move 24 and C2/D2/D3 at move 26.

## Lower fight: cut, pressure the shared escape, then secure the eyes
Opening:
1 B E5, 2 W C3, 3 B D3, 4 W C4, 5 B C5,
6 W D4, 7 B D5, 8 W E3, 9 B D2,
10 W E4, 11 B F4, 12 W F3, 13 B G4.

E3 put D3 in atari, and Black D2 extended downward. E4 joined E3 to C3/C4/D4; F3 extended into still-open lower-right space. Unlike the late E4 extension in game 8, this extension had more than one temporary destination.

14 W C7 established an upper foothold while the lower group still had options.
15 B B4, 16 W B3, 17 B C2, 18 W B2,
19 B B1, 20 W E2, 21 B E1.

B3/B2 answered the left-side pressure, but B1 undercut the first-line boundary. The group was not yet alive. After move 21, Black C2/D2/D3 had only C1/D1; Black E1 had D1/F1.

22 W F1 reduced E1 to D1. Black ignored this atari with 23 B A4.
24 W D1 captured E1 and put C2/D2/D3 in atari at C1.
Black ignored that atari with 25 B A3.
26 W C1 captured C2/D2/D3.
27 B A2 kept Black B1 in atari at A1 while connecting the left-edge Black stones.

F1 before D1 mattered. In the actual move-21 position, immediate W D1 would be a self-atari at C1; B C1 captures that stone and opens D1 for the Black group. After F1, W D1 instead captures E1, opening E1 as a second liberty for the new White stone.

Black's ignored ataris were concrete mistakes. The opening is not proven to force the played captures. A short manual alternative after W F1 is B D1 connecting E1 to C2/D2/D3; that joined five-stone Black group would have only C1, where White can capture it. This limited reading is not a proof of every alternative or a forced win.

The capture at C1 did not itself prove life. White C1/D1 and F1 were still separate from the main group, and the empty C2/D2/D3 region was connected.
28 W F2 connected F1 to E2/F3.
29 B B5, 30 W C2 connected C1/D1 through B2/C3 and closed the left boundary of D2/D3.

After move 30 the lower group had two independent secured eye spaces:
- E1: bounded by White D1/E2/F1, all connected.
- D2/D3: bounded by White D1/C2/E2/C3/E3/D4, all connected.
This life proof held when Black G3/G2/G1 closed the remaining outside liberties. The final lower group had exactly E1/D2/D3 as liberties and was alive.

White did not chase the atari Black B1 by W A1 after move 27. That would capture B1 but leave the new isolated A1 stone with only B1, introducing a simple-ko dependency. F2/C2 secured unconditional eyes elsewhere instead.

## Upper development: make the second base large enough and repair each connection
31 B G3, 32 W E7, 33 B G2, 34 W G7, 35 B G1.
The lower group stayed alive but shrank to 17 area. The earlier C7 foothold allowed White to develop the open upper side, rather than attempting another late lower-right invasion.

36 W C6, 37 B F5, 38 W D6, 39 B B6,
40 W B7, 41 B A7, 42 W A8, 43 B A6,
44 W B8, 45 B E6, 46 W D7.

B8 immediately joined A8 to B7. A8 had only B8/A9 after Black A6; leaving it disconnected would have allowed further pressure. D7 then joined the left upper chain to E7.

47 B F7 cut between E7 and G7, with only F6/F8.
48 W F8 put it in atari; 49 B F6 connected it to Black's main group.
50 W E8 connected F8 to the left upper chain.
51 B G6 left White G7 only H7/G8.
52 W G8 joined G7 to F8 before 53 B H7 removed H7.
54 W H8, 55 B H6, 56 W J8 closed the upper-right boundary.
57 B A1 connected Black B1 to the main group.
58 W D8, 59 B J7.

The choice of F8 rather than F6 at move 48 avoided a counter-atari trap: W F6 would have only G6, and B G6 could capture it, reopening F6 for Black F7. The actual F8 had E8/G8/F9 and supplied a viable connection.

## Settle the eyes before accepting the winning count
60 W B9, 61 B pass, 62 W C9, 63 B pass, 64 W pass.

B9 first connected to B8 and made a true eye at A9, bounded by A8/B9.
C9 then connected through B9 and made a second true eye at C8, bounded by B8/C7/D8/C9.
All boundaries belong to the connected upper group. D9–J9 remained a third, larger eye space.

C9 would not have connected directly to B8 or D8: those are diagonal neighbors. The actual B9–C9 sequence supplied the stone connection needed for the life proof.

The formal row/region count came late, around moves 52–63: 17 lower plus 25 upper = 42, enough to beat Black's 39 with komi. Early area estimates were provisional and were not recorded as a detailed secure/potential count around moves 10–16. Improve that timing next game; this win does not erase the counting weakness.

## Carry forward
1. Keep 20k for repeatability, especially as Black. One win does not establish consistent strength.
2. A small living group can anchor a winning total if a second base is developed while open space remains. Here 17 lower + 25 upper won; no late right-side invasion was needed.
3. Use the capture's newly opened liberty explicitly. F1 before D1 meant D1 captured E1 and survived; immediate D1 would have been captured.
4. Finish connections and eye boundaries after a capture. F2/C2 established E1 and D2/D3; the capture alone did not.
5. Repair short-liberty stones before tenuki: A8–B8, F8–E8, and G7–G8 all survived. Check the new atari stone too: F6 would have failed to G6.
6. Name actual orthogonal connections, not diagonals. B9 before C9 produced two independent true eyes A9/C8.
7. Count by rows earlier. Preserve the separation between secure area and unsecured outlines even when the opponent plays weakly.

All moves and tactical variations were chosen/read manually. Code only parsed returned current boards, counted present groups/liberties and empty regions, recorded responses, and converted the move record to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

# Game 14: White vs 20k — B+R

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
White resigned after Black move 61 (E9). All 61 moves were stone moves.
Final captures: Black 0, White 1. No pass, ko or invalid move occurred.

The 20k record is now three wins and seven losses. Retain 20k. Reading current liberties prevented some extra doomed extensions, but did not prevent two major groups from losing their bases.

## Records

- game-014.sgf contains all 61 moves and result B+R.
- game-014-log.json contains opponent selection, all 30 play responses, resignation, 31 distinct returned positions, current-board group/liberty/empty-region inventories, complete moves and counting notes.
- Final board: Black 30 stones; White 30, divided into lower-left eight, upper eight and lower-right fourteen.
- White captured Black J3 at move 44. The two endangered White groups had not yet been physically captured when White resigned.

## Lower-left: local boundary repairs did not preserve a viable base

Opening:
1 B F6, 2 W C3, 3 B D4, 4 W G3,
5 B D3, 6 W C4, 7 B C2, 8 W B3,
9 B C6, 10 W G5, 11 B G6,
12 W C7, 13 B D7, 14 W C8, 15 B B5.

After move 15, the lower-left B3/C3/C4 group had A3/B2/B4/C5. White chose 16 B4 to address the left boundary; 17 B C5 joined B5 to C6 and closed the last central route. The group then had only A3/A4/B2. It had neither two eyes nor a connection to the upper group.

18 W B2, 19 B D1, 20 W A4, 21 B A2,
22 W B1, 23 B C1, 24 W A5, 25 B A6.

B2/A4/B1 were real orthogonal connections, but their combined outcome was not life. A5 added an outside liberty A6; Black A6 immediately closed it. The eight-stone group A4/A5/B1/B2/B3/B4/C3/C4 had only A1/A3. Black A2 also had only A1/A3.

This is NOT seki. Manual current-position reading:
- B A3 leaves both the White group and Black A2/A3 with only A1.
- W A1 captures A2/A3, leaving a connected three-point interior A1/A2/A3, with White already occupying A1.
- Black moves next and plays A2, taking the dividing point. The nine-stone White group has only A3.
- W A3 captures that Black A2 stone but leaves all ten White stones with only A2.
- B A2 captures ten. There is no ko.
If White first plays A1 or A3 in the original move-25 position, Black can fill the other point and capture nine immediately.

The same strategic error as game 6 recurred, even though this session recognized the resulting shared-liberty shape correctly. Recognition after closure is too late.

A6 could not be forcibly removed by 26 W B6: that new B6 stone would have only B7. B B7 captures B6 and reopens B6 for A6 and the adjacent Black chain. The proposed atari on A6 is therefore not forcing.

Reconsider earlier, especially move 10 before further right expansion and move 16 before allowing Black C5. C5 at either opportunity is an unverified candidate to retain central access; it is not established as saving or best. Earlier lower-left eye-boundary moves are also hypotheses. The lesson is to assess the endpoint of B4/B2/A4/B1, rather than treating each connection as progress toward life.

## Upper group: expansion along a wall left one edge space

12 W C7, 14 W C8 established the upper foothold.
26 W D8, 27 B E7, 28 W E8,
35 B B7, 36 W F8, 37 B G8,
45 B B8, 48 W F7, 49 B E6,
50 W G7, 51 B H8, 52 W H7,
53 B J6, 54 W J3, 55 B J7.

D8/E8/F8/F7/G7/H7 were connected extensions. They did not create independent eye spaces. Black's B8, D7/E7/E6/F6/G6, G8/H8 and J7 closed the surrounding boundaries.

After move 55 the eight-stone group C7/C8/D8/E8/F7/F8/G7/H7 had only C9/D9/E9/F9: one connected edge strip with unsecured B9/G9 ends. Four empty points did not imply life. An eye at D9 would require C9/D8/E9 boundaries; an eye at F9 would require E9/F8/G9. The required boundary stones and their survival were never established.

56 W F1, 57 B C9, 58 W H1,
59 B D9, 60 W G2, 61 B E9.

At resignation the upper group had only F9. W F9 would be legal, but all nine stones would then have only G9. B G9 joins Black G8 and captures all nine. There is no ko or further escape.

Immediate W E9 in the move-59 position would threaten Black C9/D9 at B9, but leave White only F9; Black F9 could capture White first and reopen E9 for its own group. This is another nonforcing counter-atari.

The upper group needed a larger base and secured outside boundaries before B7/B8 and G8/H8/J7 enclosed it. Earlier upper-left boundary play or a different top development is worth examining, but no single replacement is verified. Extending toward H7 did not compensate for lost eye space.

## Lower-right: a verified living group, but too small

10 W G5, 11 B G6,
29 B H5, 30 W G4, 31 B H4,
32 W H3, 33 B J3, 34 W H2,
38 W F3, 39 B E2, 40 W F2, 41 B E3,
42 W J2, 43 B E1, 44 W J4 captured J3,
46 W J5, 47 B H6,
53 B J6, 54 W J3 connected J4/J5,
56 W F1, 58 W H1, 60 W G2.

G4 promptly connected the two-liberty G5 stone to G3. H2 and F2 kept lower access. Black E2/E3/E1 formed the outside left boundary, so White F1 was necessary for the future G1 eye.

Black ignored J3's atari at move 43. J4 captured it, opening J3 as a liberty. This was an actual opponent mistake, not a forced opening capture. J5 attempted to pressure H4/H5; Black H6 connected those stones to F6/G6 instead of allowing their capture.

J4/J5 had only J3 after B J6. White J3 immediately connected both to H3 and J2. This repair succeeded.

After G2 at move 60, all fourteen lower-right White stones were connected and had independent true eyes:
- G1: F1/G2/H1 boundaries.
- J1: H1/J2 boundaries.
All boundary stones were connected White. Black at either point captures nothing and is suicide because White retains the other eye.

This group secured sixteen area: fourteen stones plus G1/J1. By rows 1–5 it was 4, 4, 4, 2, 2 = 16. F4/F5 remained contested outside points; retaining both would make that small local outline eighteen, not a proven whole-board maximum. It could not replace the two failed bases. White resigned rather than add another stone to the forced F9/G9 capture.

## Counting: early arithmetic was sound, strategic assumptions were weak

After move 9, the log's deliberately unsecured outline was:
- Left: A/B rows 1–5 (10), plus C3/C4 (2): 12.
- Right: F–J rows 1–4 (16), plus G5/H5/J5 (3): 19.
- Total 31; no secure territory. G5 was still a planned move.

After move 15, the outline became:
- Left: A/B rows 1–4 plus C3/C4: 10.
- Top: A–C rows 7–9 (9), plus D–H rows 8–9 (10): 19.
- Right: the same 19-point outline.
- Total 48; none treated as secured.

These were disjoint geometric point sets and were explicitly provisional. The flaw was that enough concrete boundary moves and eye spaces were not identified to retain them. C5 closed the lower-left; B7/B8 and G8/H8 reduced the top; H4/J3/E2 constrained the right. The 48-point outline could not justify treating three footholds as three viable living bases.

With all 81 points assigned, White needs at least 38 area to win with seven komi; 37 draws. The final sixteen secured points were far short. No numerical final score was claimed.

## Carry forward

1. Retain 20k: three wins and seven losses. Repeated strategic enclosure persists despite reliable present-board inventories.
2. Evaluate the endpoint before making a boundary repair. B4 allowed C5 to close central access; B2/A4/B1/A5 never established two eyes.
3. Do not allow game 6's shared A1/A3 trap to form again. Read the dividing move before the opponent finishes the enclosure, not only afterward.
4. Give the upper foothold an actual eye plan before stretching along row 8/7. C9–F9 was one strip with unsecured ends, not two eyes.
5. Preserve successful prompt connections and exact life proofs: G4, F2, J3, and F1/H1/G2 maintained the right group. Count its small sixteen-point contribution honestly.

## Opening and early count: a lower framework without a winning margin

1 B C3, 2 W G7, 3 B G3, 4 W C7,
5 B C5, 6 W C6, 7 B D5, 8 W E6,
9 B E5, 10 W F5, 11 B F4, 12 W G5,

The first count, after move 8, treated the entire lower five rows as an explicitly unsecured 45-point target. That would only give the minimum Black winning split. No current group was called alive or territory secure.

After move 14, the revised outline was only 41: rows 1–4 all nine each (36), plus A–E in row 5 (five). White F5/G5/H5 occupied the rest of that boundary, and J5 was excluded. This count correctly showed the need for more space.

D6 and B6 added two retained points in row 6. B5 immediately connected the two-liberty B6 stone to C5; A5 prevented the left undercut and White A7 connected A6 upward. E4 joined the C5/D5/E5 chain to F4/G4/G3. H3 blocked the right descent; J2 put J3 in atari, White J4 connected upward, and H2 promptly joined J2 to the main group. C4 connected C3.

However, White H4/J4/J3 removed three points from the earlier lower outline. After move 32 it was 40:
- Rows 1–2: nine each = 18.
- Row 3: eight, excluding White J3.
- Row 4: seven, A–G.
- Row 5: five, A–E.
- Row 6: B6/D6, two.
Total 40, still provisional until the later invasions were settled.

The eventual score did not arise from losing the lower group. This framework itself was too small. With 40 against 41 plus komi, shifting four White points to Black would only draw; shifting five would win B+2. Development around moves 9–15 needed to contest more than the two retained row-6 points, or establish a second viable base earlier. No single opening replacement is verified. E5/D6 were not shown individually wrong, and this opening is not established as losing against every reply.

## Top entry: eye hopes were blocked, then a diagonal liberty was imagined

33 B F8, 34 W G8,
35 B E8, 36 W D8,
37 B F7, 38 W F9,
39 B H1, 40 W E9 captured E8/F7/F8.

Before F8, prospective E9/G9 eyes were named, requiring D9/F9/H9 and E8/G8 boundaries. These were needed future stones, not secure eyes. White G8 immediately denied the proposed right boundary. E8 tried to expand left, but White D8 closed that side. After move 36 the two-stone group had exactly E9/F7/F9.

The decisive reading mistake was F7. The session imagined it might add a G6 escape route and attack the separated White chains. But F7's orthogonal neighbors are E7, G7, F6 and F8. G6 is diagonal. E7/G7/F6 were all White; F8 was already Black. F7 added NO liberty and reduced the group to E9/F9. White F9 then left only E9.

This is more concrete than a general life-planning failure: the current inventory contradicted the imagined extension. Before playing an escape move, list its actual empty orthogonal neighbors and check that at least one route is added. F7 was not forcing and could have been omitted.

Manual reading after move 38:
- B E9 has only D9 for the entire four-stone group; W D9 captures all four immediately.
- Alternatively B E9, W G9, B D9 adds C9 as the only liberty; W C9 captures five.
These lines do not prove every earlier F8 replacement fails. They establish that the chosen continuation had no demonstrated rescue and that extending along the first line would add doomed stones against the stated replies.

The in-game log initially included an invalid branch after B E9/W D9, imagining Black could next capture F9 with G9. That ignored White D9's immediate four-stone capture and the liberties it opens. A final correction explicitly discards that branch. Do not inherit it as a valid variation.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.

Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko.
